metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic, specifically isolating trials where TTB and Tallying make strictly opposing predictions (e.g., one option wins on the single most valid feature, while the other wins on a greater number of less valid features). For a simulated TTB agent, this proportion will be close to 1.0 (subject to epsilon noise). For a simulated Tallying agent, this proportion will be close to 0.0, as it reliably chooses the opposite option. This creates an enormous mean gap with very low between-subject variance.

By design, all trials in this experiment pit the Tallying heuristic directly against the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. Tallying always favors the option with the greater total number of positive features, while TTB always favors the opposite option (which wins on the single most valid discriminating cue). This metric simply computes the proportion of a subject's choices that align with the Tallying prediction. Under the Tallying theory, this proportion will be close to 1. Under the TTB theory, it will be close to 0. The gap is maximized, and within-theory variance is minimized.

This metric isolates trials where Take The Best (TTB) and Tallying strictly conflict (i.e., one option is favored by the most valid cue, but the other option has more total positive cues). On these conflict trials, it calculates the proportion of times the subject chose the option favored by TTB. The Advocated Theory (pure TTB) predicts subjects will systematically choose the TTB option on these trials, yielding a mean significantly greater than 0.5. The Competing Theory assumes a mixture of TTB and Tallying with the probability of using TTB bounded between 0.4 and 0.6, meaning it predicts subjects will be close to indifferent on these conflict trials, yielding a mean very close to 0.5.

This metric isolates the 'strict conflict' trials where Take The Best (TTB) favors one option (based on the highest-validity discriminating cue) while Tallying favors the other option (based on the sheer number of winning cues). The Pure TTB theory predicts that subjects will consistently choose the TTB-favored option on these trials (predicting a metric close to 1.0). In contrast, the Strategy Mixture theory posits that individuals probabilistically alternate between TTB and Tallying, predicting that subjects will choose the TTB-favored option only around 50% of the time (determined by their p_ttb parameter). Computing the proportion of TTB-consistent choices on these specific trials yields a large, stable gap between the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses the option [0, 1, 1, 0, 0] over [1, 0, 0, 1, 1]. In these specific trials, the Mixture model (TTB + Tallying) strongly prefers [1, 0, 0, 1, 1] because it has the single most valid cue AND a greater total number of positive cues. However, the Advocated WADD model strongly prefers [0, 1, 1, 0, 0] because the exponentiated sum of the second and third most valid cues outweighs the first cue. This creates a maximal divergence between the two theories: the Mixture model predicts a value near 0, while WADD predicts a value near 1.

This metric calculates the difference in preference for the option with more features on two specific trial types. On Trial 1 ([1,0,0,1,1] vs [0,1,1,0,0]), the Strategy Mixture model strongly prefers the first option (~90% probability) since both Take The Best (TTB) and Tallying agree. However, WADD slightly prefers the second option due to the compensatory weights of the second and third validities. On Trial 2 ([0,1,1,1,1] vs [1,0,0,0,0]), TTB and Tallying conflict, resulting in a ~50% choice rate for the first option under the Mixture model, whereas WADD consistently prefers the first option because the summed exponentiated weights outcompete the top cue. The difference P(Target 1) - P(Target 2) is expected to be highly positive for the Mixture model and strongly negative for the WADD model, maximizing discriminability while remaining stable within subjects.

Focuses on Trial 1 and Trial 2, where Option B has 4 positive features (cues 3, 4, 5, 6) and Option A has 2 positive features (cues 1, 2 or 1, 3). The Competing Theory (Top-K Tallying, K in 1,2,3) predicts Option A will be chosen almost exclusively because Option A dominates in the top validity cues. However, the Advocated Theory (WADD with exponentiated validities) predicts Option B will be chosen because the combined weighted value of four lower-validity cues surpasses the two higher-validity cues. The metric simply computes the proportion of times Option B is chosen on these critical trials.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the deterministic predictions of the WADD model. For Trials 1 and 2, WADD predicts the option with 4 lower-validity features, whereas Top-K Tallying deterministically predicts the option with 2 higher-validity features (0% alignment). For Trials 3 through 6, WADD deterministically favors the option that strictly dominates on lower-validity features, whereas Top-K Tallying is blind to these features and predicts a 50/50 tie (50% alignment). Consequently, WADD will score > 0.5 on this metric (approaching 1.0 for high beta/low epsilon), while Top-K Tallying will score around 0.333 (or up to 0.5 under pure random guessing). This establishes a robust and consistent theoretical gap.

We compute the choice proportion for options that are favored by the Compensatory (WADD) strategy but are involved in strict heuristic conflict. Specifically, we look at trials comparing [1,1,0,0,0] vs [0,0,1,1,1] and [1,0,0,0,0] vs [0,1,1,1,1]. In these trials, Take The Best and Tallying point in opposite directions, causing the Competing Theory (Conflict-Induced Guessing) to predict exactly 50% choice probability. However, the Advocated Theory (WADD with exponentiated validities) consistently predicts a preference for [1,1,0,0,0] and [0,1,1,1,1], respectively, across all allowed parameter values. Thus, the metric will closely hover around 0.5 for the Competing Theory (with variance purely due to binomial noise) and be significantly > 0.5 for the Advocated Theory.

This metric calculates the proportion of times Option A is chosen on Trial 2 (where A=[0,1,1,1,1] and B=[1,0,0,0,0]). Under the Advocated theory, this is a strict conflict trial (TTB favors B, Tallying favors A), leading to random guessing and a choice proportion of ~0.5. Under the Competing theory, the combined exponentiated weights of A's four cues easily surpass B's single cue, leading to a strong deterministic preference for A (proportion ~1.0).
